summary:
Busan stands under the national framework of South Korea: gender identity and gender expression are not criminalised in civilian life, and consensual same-sex conduct between civilians is legal. Nothing in the available sources documents a Busan-specific ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern concerning trans people, so a visitor in this metropolitan city is assessed against the national picture.

Legal gender recognition exists and its surgical prerequisite has fallen away. On 8 May 2024 a regional court in Yeongdong approved registered-sex changes from male to female for five applicants who had not undergone sex-reassignment surgery, holding that determining gender change by surgery is contrary to law and that judicial guidelines requiring surgery now serve as reference rather than criteria. The court stated that every human being has the right to form their character and live a life according to their gender identity.

Trans visitors have a judicially enforced right to public restrooms. Police advised a person transitioning from male to female, whose family-register gender change had been approved by a court in 2020, to avoid women's public restrooms. The Seoul Central District Court held that this advice infringed personal rights, and on 22 July 2024 the Seoul appellate court dismissed the state's appeal, finalising 300,000 won in damages against a 3 million won claim and holding that comfortable restroom use is a fundamental and universal human right.

The ruling sits against a documented pattern of fear-driven avoidance. A 2021 survey by the National Human Rights Commission of Korea of 591 transgender respondents found 41% using a restroom of a different gender, 39% avoiding food and drink in order to do so, and 36% forgoing restroom use altogether.
tangentialFactors:
Sub-national courts have enforced restroom access against private operators as well as against the state. In 2021 the Daegu District Court, Pohang branch, awarded 7 million won against a beauty academy that prohibited a transgender student from using its restroom. That case is a single provincial data point illustrating a national pattern, not a Busan-specific finding.

The surrounding context still requires care. South Korea has no comprehensive anti-discrimination law covering sexual orientation or gender identity, so services, employment and accommodation carry no statutory protection on those grounds. Organised conservative opposition is active, and Human Rights Watch's 2025 world report records persistent documented discrimination against LGBT people while noting a relatively positive overall record for free media and civil society. No severe incident involving a trans visitor is documented in these sources.
localsOnly:
Residents share the recognition route the courts have opened. The May 2024 ruling removed surgery as a condition of registered-sex change, and the Supreme Court has allowed a transgender person with minor children to change their gender in the family relations register.

Transgender people are excluded from South Korean military service altogether. Within the armed forces, Military Criminal Act article 92-6 criminalises consensual same-sex conduct among personnel with up to two years' imprisonment; the Constitutional Court upheld the provision in 2023, and a gay soldier received a six-month sentence in 2017.

Healthcare carries no statutory protection on gender-identity grounds. In November 2023 the National Human Rights Commission of Korea flagged a transgender blind spot in hospitalisation after the Ministry of Health and Welfare rejected a request to draft hospitalisation guidelines for transgender patients, reasoning that accommodating diverse circumstances is difficult.

There is no same-sex marriage in South Korea, which matters to a resident travelling with a partner. The Constitutional Court's 2024 ruling extended recognition only in the specific area of same-sex partners' healthcare rights.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in this inventory addresses Busan's own metropolitan ordinances, local police practice, or facility access within the city. The restroom and recognition findings are national in scope or drawn from other provinces, and their application to Busan follows from the unitary national framework rather than from local verification.

The 300,000 won award was assessed against a 3 million won claim, so the sum functions as symbolic compensation rather than a measure of harm. Whether the July 2024 appellate decision has produced revised state guidance on police advice to trans people is unresolved in these sources.

Whether Busan has specific LGBTQ+ venues, local advocacy organisations, or documented local hostility remains unsourced here. The assessment of on-the-ground conditions rests on national survey data and reporting about established neighbourhoods in the capital.
